description: We’re software engineers building health monitoring software for astronauts. Our offline-first system tracks fatigue, sleep disruption and stress and flags problems without contact with Earth, vital on Mars missions where communication is delayed. We cover backend, frontend and data pipelines and prototype fast. Join us for a clear plan, focused scope and a polished demo. Looking for: a health/biomedical background, a UI/UX designer, an ML/data person, and a strong presenter.
summary:
VITALIS is an offline-first health monitoring app that helps astronauts on long Moon and Mars missions track their own health, spot problems early and know what to do next.

What we developed: Astronauts log heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep and mood, and record symptoms on an interactive body map. VITALIS compares each reading with the person’s own baseline, shows animated trend charts, and raises colour coded alerts that explain why they fired. Offline guidance, reminders and progress tracking help crews act early.

How it addresses the challenge: Each of NASA’s five spaceflight hazards has a matching feature: space-weather context from NASA DONKI for radiation, mood and sleep tracking for isolation, offline operation for distance from Earth, trend tracking for gravity-related changes, and environment readings for closed habitats.

Why it matters: On deep-space missions, help is delayed and crews must watch their own health. VITALIS makes that easier and keeps working without a connection. It supports decisions and does not diagnose.
details:
Project Link:

https://astronaut-health-monitoring-system-lemon.vercel.app/

What does it do and how does it work?

VITALIS is a health monitoring app for astronauts on long Moon and Mars missions. The astronaut logs heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep and mood, and records symptoms by tapping a body map. Each new reading goes through an alert engine with three checks: a safe range, deviation from that astronaut’s own baseline, and multi-day trends. The result shows as a colour-coded status (normal, caution, warning or critical) with an explanation of why it fired and a link to plain-language guidance. Charts draw themselves to show how values change over days and weeks. Other screens cover sleep, mood check-ins, habitat environment and radiation context, reminders, records with CSV or PDF export, and a Hazards Learn Hub. The app works offline, so logging, charts, alerts and guidance keep working with no connection to Earth, and records sync when a connection returns.

What benefits does it have?

Small drifts are caught early, even when a value still looks normal by general standards.

Physical and mental health are tracked together.

Guidance is understandable without a doctor present.

The interface suits tablets, gloves and low-light cabins, with dark and light themes.

It keeps working with no connection.

What is the intended impact?

Crews on Artemis and Mars missions will manage much of their own health for months, with delayed communication and limited equipment. VITALIS aims to make that safer by turning raw numbers into early, understandable signals while leaving medical decisions to professionals. The same approach could help other isolated settings on Earth, such as polar stations, ships and remote clinics.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did you use?

React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS for the front end, built as an installable web app, with browser storage for offline use. Python FastAPI with a SQLite database for the back end. Figma and Figma Make for design, VS Code with GitHub Copilot for code review and fixes, and Claude for planning and documentation. NASA resources used as references included the Human Research Program hazard definitions, NASA-STD-3001, OSDR and the DONKI space-weather event format. No special hardware is required, only a browser on a tablet or computer.

How is it creative?

It compares each astronaut with their own baseline instead of one population average.

The Hazards Learn Hub ties NASA’s five hazards directly to the tools that address them.

Charts animate as they load, so a trend is visible as it forms.

Critical alerts are calm and readable rather than flashing.

Light and dark themes can follow the habitat’s day and night cycle.

Streaks and badges encourage regular check-ins without shaming.

What factors did your team consider?

Safety: the app supports decisions and never diagnoses. Serious readings always point to the flight surgeon, and alert thresholds are editable and need clinical review.

Connectivity: offline operation for communication delays.

Accessibility: large touch targets, adjustable text size, and status shown by icon and text as well as colour.

Honesty about data: no public source gives real astronaut vitals or personal radiation dose, so most of the data in the demo is simulated and labelled as such.

Privacy: PIN login and separate crew profiles for sensitive health records.

Mental health: mood, stress and sleep get the same attention as physical vitals.
dataRefs: NASA Human Research Program, Hazards of Human Spaceflight
